Artist Casey Curran creates kinetic sculptures that combine mechanical systems with forms inspired by plants and natural structures. In this prototype, layers of delicate petals are connected so that a single mechanical action produces a rippling movement across the entire structure. Instead of every element moving independently, the motion travels through the sculpture like a wave. This type of movement is central to Curran’s practice. Using motors, wires, cranks and carefully engineered mechanisms, he creates artificial flowers and organisms that bloom, flutter and contract.  The machinery is artificial, but the movement feels strangely organic ,engineering becomes a way of imitating the rhythms of living systems. #art #artist #fashion #avantgarde #design

This one starts out as a very orderly blue grid and ends up feeling like a cutaway view into a hidden room. Everything is colored with sand: the outer cube, the inner walls, and the pink floor tiles tucked into the center. What makes it work so well is the contrast — cool blue on the outside, warmer pink details inside, all locked into that clean perspective. It lands somewhere between pixel architecture, a tiny tiled room, and an impossible object. I especially like that it doesn’t need motion to feel dimensional. The structure does all the work. ✨ Did you know you can make DIY taste-safe kinetic sand with simple ingredients from your pantry? It's non-toxic, budget-friendly, and perfect for toddlers! My 3-year-old often stays busy for an hour playing with it—molding shapes, digging treasures, and pretending to bake "cakes."  Ingredients You’ll Need: 1 cup baking soda 1/2 cup cornstarch 1/2 cup sugar 2–4 tablespoons warm water  (mix with food coloring of your choice) 1 tablespoon cream of tartar Step-by-Step Instructions: Mix the dry ingredients In a large mixing bowl, combine the baking soda, cornstarch, sugar, and cream of tartar. Stir until evenly distributed. Prepare the colored water In a small bowl, add a few drops of food coloring to the warm water. Adjust the intensity of the color by adding more or fewer drops. Combine wet and dry ingredients Gradually add the colored water to the dry mixture, 1 tablespoon at a time. Mix with a spoon or your hands until the sand reaches your desired consistency—moist and moldable, but not sticky. You may not need all the water, so add it slowly! Test and play Once the mixture holds its shape when squeezed, it’s ready for playtime! If it feels too dry, add a few drops of water. If it’s too sticky, sprinkle in a bit more cornstarch. Thomas D. Westergaard is a Danish designer and founder of Ceremoni Studio, where he transforms the traditional candle into a kinetic sculpture. Instead of treating wax as a static object, he engineers candles that bend, twist, and weave together as they burn. Every prototype is tested through long time-lapse recordings to study the flame, the melting wax, and the structure, refining each design until movement and combustion become one. His work sits somewhere between industrial design, engineering, and performance. #art #artist #avantgarde #candles #timelapse

A machine that goes nowhere — endlessly moving through time. Günther Uecker’s 'Sand Mill' consists of a slowly rotating mechanism that continuously drags through sand, leaving and erasing traces in an endless cycle. Uecker first created a "Sand Mill" in 1965, and the work became part of his wider exploration of movement, time, repetition and impermanence. He has described the 'Sand Mill' as "the grinding of time" — a poetic image for existence gradually passing away. The marks in the sand also connect to his childhood growing up on a farm, where he experienced the cycles of nature, while his encounters with Japan and Zen gardens brought another influence: an apparently still landscape that is nevertheless constantly changing. The Arp Museum in Bahnhof is currently showing a particularly large example from the 'Sand Mill' series (1969/2014). Nothing is created. Nothing is completed. The movement simply continues. . #KineticArt #MinimalArt #Museum #News #ContemporaryArt
